close.title: Let’s Build the Way In.
close.sub: IP-extension partnerships · Co-productions with immersive in the plan from day one

a.title:
Old Stories,
New Doors
a.subtitle: What five winters of A Christmas Carol VR taught us about classic IP
a.thesis: Beloved stories need new audiences and new revenue beyond the stage and screen. Live immersive theater is a working model for the audience half, and the right partnership supplies the rest.
a.takeaway: The curtain comes down. The story doesn’t have to.

b.title:
Engine Mastery
× Craft
b.subtitle: Why the studios winning in immersive need both
b.thesis: The companies winning in immersive pair engine mastery with craft: photoreal work that runs on the hardware audiences actually have, built by people who know how to give an audience a role.
b.takeaway: Craft makes them care. Engineering makes sure they can.

pool.title:
Every Beloved Story
Hits the Same Ceiling.
bullets: The run ends. The season closes. The house only has so many seats.
The audience that loves it is getting older, and the next one needs a new way in.
Classic IP needs new audiences and new revenue beyond the stage and the screen.
pool.tags: IP value · Audience development · New revenue
pool.notes: Everyone in this room knows this math. You have a story people love. But a run ends, a release window closes, a theater only has so many seats, and the audience that grew up with the story is getting older. The question isn't whether the story still works. It's where the next audience meets it, and who pays for that meeting. We spent five winters working on that question with one very old story.

pool.title: Agile Lens: Immersive Design
pool.bigCaption: New York · Real-time studio · Theater, culture and luxury brands
pool.notes: I'm Alex Coulombe. Agile Lens is a New York immersive studio: more than a hundred spatial experiences shipped since 2016, all built in real time.

pool.title: It Started as a Small Ask
pool.subtitle: With Actors Theatre of Louisville · 2021
bullets: Actors Theatre of Louisville asked us for production assets: digital characters and some video.
We came back with a bigger idea: a full live production of A Christmas Carol, in VR.
They said yes, then gave us their blessing to remount it every year.
pool.notes: In 2021, Actors Theatre of Louisville asked us for production assets. Digital characters, some video. Not a VR show. We did the research and came back with a bigger idea: if we're building the sets, the characters and the costumes anyway, why not stage the whole thing, live, in virtual reality? They said yes, and then gave us their blessing to remount it every year. That's the part I want producers to hear: the theater didn't hand off its story. It extended it, with a partner, into a new format.

pool.title: A Christmas Carol VR
pool.subtitle: Live actors. Live audiences. One shared virtual stage.
bullets: Live actors with facial and motion capture perform on the streets of a virtual Victorian London
Fully remote: actors, crew and audience each join from wherever they are
Five holiday seasons, 2021–2025 · [FILL: total performances and total audience]
pool.notes: Here's what it was. A Christmas Carol, performed live inside virtual reality. Live actors, with facial and motion capture, performing on the streets of a virtual Victorian London: Ari Tarr as Dickens, Scrooge and others, Debbie Deer as the Ghosts, directed for VR by David Gochfeld. It's fully remote. The actors, the crew and the audience are all in different places, and they share one stage. Forty-five minutes, a curtain time, a house. We ran it for five holiday seasons, 2021 through 2025. [FILL: total performances and audience. The FMX deck lists '150+ shows'; confirm it is a five-season total before saying it.]
This is the audience's view. Not row M of a theater: inside the room, with the characters.

pool.title: How Audiences Experienced It
pool.subtitle: Not watching a story. Standing inside one.
bullets: Eye contact: the actor sees you, and plays the scene to you
AI Dickens, a digital host voiced with the lead actor’s permission, welcomes guests before curtain
After the show, a live Q&A with the actors
pool.notes: What did it feel like? Intimate. Scrooge can turn and look you in the eye, because the actor can actually see you. Before curtain, guests are welcomed by AI Dickens, a digital host built with our lead actor's voice, cloned with his permission and paid for, so the human performer can save his energy for the show. And afterwards the actors stay for a live Q&A. The audience isn't watching a recording of a play. They're part of a night that only happens once.

pool.title: What It Proved About Classic IP
bullets: A story audiences already love lowers the barrier to a brand-new format
A live show without a building: the house can be anywhere
The value outlived the run: characters, sets, an AI host and live-performance tools we reuse
pool.notes: So what did five winters prove? One: familiarity is an asset. A story people already love lowers the barrier to trying something new. Two: the house can be anywhere. A live show doesn't need a building, so the audience isn't limited to who can get to one. [FILL: one sentence on reach, if you have a number you trust.] Three: the value wasn't only the show. The characters, the sets, the AI host and the live-performance pipeline carried into our next projects. And I'll be candid about what it didn't prove on its own: we made work that taught us a lot and still needed a different funding and distribution model. A strong experience needs a partner who understands how its audience finds it.
pool.subtitle: Five winters, three lessons

pool.title:
The Show Closed.
The Assets Didn’t.
pool.subtitle: December 2025
bullets: The final shows were fully booked a week before closing
The final performance was captured in 3D and can be replayed from any seat
Its rehearsal and live-performance tools now power our other theater work
pool.notes: We closed it in December 2025, after five seasons, and the final shows were fully booked a week out. But the work didn't disappear. We captured the final performance in 3D, so it can be replayed from any seat in the house: a live show with a second life. pool.title: Royal Shakespeare Company
pool.subtitle: Virtual rehearsal tools, developed with the RSC
bullets: Actors rehearse in a 1:1 scan of the Swan Theatre; directors follow along from a laptop
Built with theater people, for theater people: the script stays in your hand, like paper
An R&D grant with XR Network+, 2024–2025: tested with drama students, shown in Stratford
pool.notes: With the Royal Shakespeare Company, through an R&D grant with XR Network+, we developed virtual rehearsal tools: a one-to-one laser scan of the Swan Theatre in Stratford that actors can rehearse inside, while directors follow from a laptop. On the left, the real Swan; on the right, ours. We tried every clever way to float a script in space. Every actor wanted the same thing: a script they could hold, and put down on the floor. Same as paper. Respect the craft, and the technology disappears.

pool.title: Heavenue
pool.bigCaption: Our cloud platform for live performance in virtual space: A Christmas Carol’s first season, then The Orchard Off-Broadway
pool.notes: Because we kept needing it, we built Heavenue: a cloud platform for live performance in virtual space. Its first show was Carol's first season. Then The Orchard, Off-Broadway, a Chekhov production with Mikhail Baryshnikov and Jessica Hecht, where we built the virtual side: the same performance on a physical stage and in VR at once. pool.title:
Beautiful Demos Are Easy.
Shipping Them Isn’t.
bullets: Immersive work lives or dies in the gap between the trailer and the headset
Engine mastery: it runs, beautifully, on the hardware audiences actually have
Craft: once they’re inside, they care
pool.notes: Most of you have seen a gorgeous immersive trailer for something that never reached an audience, or reached one and stuttered. That gap is where immersive projects live or die. The companies winning in this space do two things at once. Engine mastery: the work runs, beautifully, on the hardware audiences actually own. And craft: once people are inside, they care. Either one alone isn't enough.

pool.title: Photoreal That Actually Runs
pool.subtitle: Heavy scenes, real hardware
bullets: We optimized photoreal digital humans to run on standalone headsets
That moved A Christmas Carol VR from gaming PCs to headsets audiences already own
Increasing access is worth the work, as long as the artistic vision survives
pool.notes: Here's what engine mastery buys you. We optimized photoreal digital humans to run on standalone headsets, no gaming PC required. In 2024 that moved Christmas Carol onto headsets people already own, and that season had our biggest show yet. Our rule: increasing access is always worth the work, as long as the artistic vision survives the trip.

pool.title: Royal Caribbean · Perfect Day Mexico
pool.bigText:
Six guests. One sky.
No internet required.
pool.bigCaption: A shared hot-air-balloon ride on standalone headsets, fully offline, run from an operator tablet · 1,000+ riders
pool.notes: And it has to run where the audience is. For Royal Caribbean we built a hot-air-balloon ride for six guests at once, on standalone headsets, fully offline, run by staff from a tablet. More than a thousand riders, and one motion-sickness incident. Reset time, staff training and battery plans sound unglamorous. On a ship, they decide how many guests ride.

pool.title: Four Seasons Private Residences
pool.subtitle: Lake Austin: luxury homes, toured from a headset
bullets: Buyers walk full-scale, photoreal residences years before they’re built
A wireless holodeck, 82 by 65 feet: families tour together, no cables
We built it, set it up, and ran its first six months of operation
pool.notes: Four Seasons Private Residences in Lake Austin. Buyers put on a headset and walk the residence: the light, the view, the finishes, years before it exists. We built a wireless holodeck, 82 by 65 feet, so a family can tour together with no cables, and we staffed and ran its first six months. As I said on Voices of VR: it's binary. Without this VR experience, the project would not be happening. And that's the pattern we see again and again: photoreal, client-branded demos turn foot traffic into qualified conversations.

pool.title:
What Kind of Partnerships
Are We Looking For?
pool.tagline: Two kinds. Both start with a story you already own or produce.
pool.notes: Which brings me to the question our moderator asked: what kind of partnerships are we looking for? Two kinds, and both start with a story you already own or produce.

pool.title: 1 · IP-extension partnerships
pool.subtitle: With producers and rights holders
pool.bigText:
Bring the story.
We’ll build the way in.
pool.bigCaption: An immersive edition of a world audiences already love: live, location-based, or at home
pool.notes: First: IP-extension partnerships with producers and rights holders. You bring a story world audiences already love. We design and build the immersive edition: a live performance, a location-based experience, something people take home on a headset. The rights stay yours; the audience gets a new door. That's how Carol began: a theater extending its holiday classic with a partner.

pool.title: 2 · Co-productions from day one
pool.subtitle: Immersive inside the financing and distribution plan
pool.bigText:
In the plan,
not bolted on after.
pool.bigCaption: Budgeted with the production: new windows, new audiences, assets that carry across formats
pool.notes: Second: co-productions where immersive is part of the financing and distribution plan from day one, not bolted on after picture lock. When the immersive edition is in the first budget, the digital sets, characters and performances get built once and used everywhere, and the immersive release becomes another window and another audience, not a marketing afterthought. That's the lesson Carol taught us: the experience was strong; what it needed was a partner with the audience and the distribution plan from the start.

pool.title: How we start
pool.bigText:
One story.
One audience.
One prototype.
pool.bigCaption: A short, paid prototype of a single audience moment, then a production plan you can finance
pool.notes: And we start small. One story, one audience, one prototype: a short, paid prototype of a single moment an audience would have in your world. Then a production plan you can actually finance. Come find us in the demo area today and we'll show you what that moment feels like.

The story doesn’t have to.
